blocks.content: The cdn topic covered spreading content geographically to reduce distance. This topic covers a genuinely different, equally important scaling problem: spreading INCOMING TRAFFIC across multiple servers running the exact same application, so no single server has to handle the entire load alone.
Nearly every real, large scale application you have ever used sits behind a load balancer, quietly and invisibly distributing traffic across many servers working together.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437995014-129532804.png
1. The Real Problem: One Server Has a Hard Ceiling
blocks.text: 1. The Real Problem: One Server Has a Hard Ceiling

blocks.content: A single server, no matter how powerful, has a genuine, hard ceiling on how much traffic it can actually handle at once. Push past that ceiling, and the server becomes overloaded, genuinely slow, or simply goes down entirely, taking the whole application with it.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437995014-290884571.png
blocks.alt: The Real Problem: One Server Has a Hard Ceiling

blocks.content: 2. The Fix: Spreading Traffic Across Many Servers
blocks.text: 2. The Fix: Spreading Traffic Across Many Servers

blocks.content: A load balancer sits in front of multiple servers all running the exact same application, and distributes incoming traffic across all of them. This gives an application far more total capacity than any single server could ever provide alone, a technique commonly called horizontal scaling.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437995015-42634890.png
blocks.alt: The Fix: Spreading Traffic Across Many Servers

blocks.content: 3. How a Load Balancer Actually Decides Where to Send Traffic
blocks.text: 3. How a Load Balancer Actually Decides Where to Send Traffic

blocks.content: Several real, common algorithms decide exactly how incoming requests get distributed. Round robin simply cycles through the available servers in order, one after another. Least connections specifically sends a new request to whichever server currently has the fewest active connections, genuinely balancing based on real current load. IP hash consistently routes the same client to the same server every time, useful when a specific server needs to remember something about that particular client.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437995015-714960929.png
blocks.alt: How a Load Balancer Actually Decides Where to Send Traffic

4. Health Checks: Automatically Avoiding Failing Servers
blocks.text: 4. Health Checks: Automatically Avoiding Failing Servers

blocks.content: A load balancer regularly checks whether each server behind it is actually healthy and responding correctly. If a specific server starts failing these checks, it is automatically removed from rotation, and traffic is routed only to the servers that are genuinely still healthy, without any human needing to intervene manually in the moment.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437995015-574303768.png
blocks.alt: Health Checks: Automatically Avoiding Failing Servers

blocks.title: This is a real, continuous, automated process
blocks.content: Health checks are not a one time setup step, they run continuously, meaning a load balancer can detect and route around a server failure within moments of it actually happening.
5. A Genuine Resilience Benefit, Not Just Capacity
blocks.text: 5. A Genuine Resilience Benefit, Not Just Capacity

blocks.content: Beyond raw capacity, this design provides real resilience too. If one server genuinely goes down entirely, the others simply keep serving traffic normally, and the application as a whole stays up and available, rather than the entire system failing because of one single server problem.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437995015-915252662.png
blocks.alt: A Genuine Resilience Benefit, Not Just Capacity

blocks.content: 6. Layer 4 Versus Layer 7 Load Balancing

A Layer 4 load balancer makes its routing decisions based only on IP address and port information, fast and simple. A Layer 7 load balancer can actually look at real HTTP content, the request path, specific headers, letting it make genuinely smarter, more flexible routing decisions, at the cost of a bit more processing overhead per request.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437995015-5391415.png

7. A Real World Analogy

A traffic cop directing cars at a genuinely busy intersection captures this well, actively spreading cars across multiple available lanes instead of letting them all pile up into one single, badly jammed lane, keeping traffic flowing smoothly overall even though the total volume of cars stays exactly the same.

blocks.title: A forward pointer within this module
blocks.content: Load balancers are often used alongside a reverse proxy, covered in the very next topic in this module, the two concepts are closely related and frequently implemented together in real systems.
8. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways

items: Assuming a load balancer only exists to increase raw capacity, when it also provides a genuine, real resilience benefit if one server fails.
Assuming every load balancer works the same way, when Layer 4 and Layer 7 balancing make genuinely different tradeoffs between speed and routing intelligence.
A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers running the same application.
Different algorithms, round robin, least connections, IP hash, decide traffic distribution in genuinely different ways.
Continuous health checks automatically route traffic away from a failing server, without manual intervention.
